The article is missing something that I call the triple compromise accommodation. How does society bridge the gap between the jobs that need doing and the jobs that people want to do. Part one of the triple compromise accommodation is wage rises and wage cuts. Try to attract people to the jobs that need doing. But we are making a deduction here: the shops are running out of bread because there is a shortage of bakers. Rather than raise the wages of bakers we could raise the price of bread.

Adjusting wages is the first part of the triple compromise accommodation, and adjusting prices is the second part. The third part is different in kind from the first to two parts. Part three is an accounting convention. Keep the accounts for different products separately and fund the higher wages for bakers from the higher prices for bread. Look for a compromise. If the shortfall is 10%, try a 5% price rise and a 5% wage rise.

Part three works both ways. If perishable stuff is going to waste because if doesn't sell, try cutting the price, to shift it. Cut wages too, workers are more needed elsewhere. A little of each, economising on wages to fund the price cut.

Notice that tradition treats the concept of the free market as an atomic concept. I treat the concept of the free market as a compound concept. One part is the triple compromise accommodation. The other part of the free market is the private ownership of the means of production. The free market is the triple compromise accommodation plus one particular vision of who is adjusting the prices and wages and why they do what they do. In the free market, the bourgeoisie are adjusting prices and wages, motivated by private profit and constrained by the mobility of consumers and workers in the markets for goods and labour.

Now we can ask: what becomes of the triple compromise accommodation when Marxism abolishes the private ownership of the means of production? A non-Marxist revolution could continue to use the triple compromise accommodation, with the central planning system taking reports from shops about goods selling out and responding by adjusting prices and wages. Meanwhile the Bureau of Labour routinely approves requests by workers to change jobs, or to take a training course with a view to moving to a better paid job later. But a Marxist revolution cannot do this.

Marxism rejects the cash nexus. Society is supposed to planned. The central planning system is supposed to be in charge. If the plan is responding to common people making individual choices between goods and between jobs, based on individual choices about prices and wages, the revolution recreates the many of the despised market outcomes that the revolutionaries were revolting against. Marxism rejects the triple compromise accommodation.

Thus Marxist societies are not incentive compatible. Does that mean that they don't work? Not so fast. There is a damaging mismatch between the jobs that need doing and the jobs that people want to do but Marxist don't have to give up; they can resort to coercion. The descent of Marxist societies into totalitarian hell holes is a multi-step process. First comes the rejection of the triple compromise accommodation. That makes the economy breakdown, so second comes coercion. That requires institutions to force people to do things that they are reluctant to do. Shortage of bread? You there! Become a baker or you'll be taken out and shot!

Once the institutions of coercion are in place, psychopaths rise to the top and commence a rain of terror. But there is something inevitable about this. Once the revolution rejects the triple compromise accommodation, the next two steps are forced.
